content:
I've been formalizing the N=1 chiral scalar sector in Physlib, the complex-geometry machinery behind supersymmetric scalar field theories, from the calculus foundations up to a worked example. I'm learning SUSY as I formalize it, so comments, corrections, and pointers are very much appreciated. The full foundation is on the susy branch (#1107), going into master in small review-sized pieces. The first piece, the chiral indexing layer, is #1113, and it's live for review now.

What's in the stack:

  • Wirtinger calculus. The holomorphic and anti-holomorphic derivatives ∂/∂z and ∂/∂z̄, built abstractly over Mathlib and then specialized to a complex coordinate basis. It's index-agnostic, so SUSY is just one place it gets used.
  • The chiral sector. Chiral and anti-chiral labels are kept as two distinct index types tied by an explicit bijection, so the two slots of the metric can never be confused. There's a single physical field configuration; the anti-chiral scalars are its complex conjugates, not independent data.
  • Kähler potential. A real-valued function whose reality is enforced by its type rather than a side condition.
  • Kähler metric g_{IJ̄} = ∂_I ∂_J̄ K, with hermiticity proven for any potential. That real-codomain choice is what makes the proof clean: it comes out of Schwarz's theorem plus reality of the complex lift.
  • Superpotential. A globally holomorphic function W, with its conjugate W̄ bundled as anti-holomorphic.
  • Worked example. The log Kähler potential K = -∑_I log(i(φ̄ᴵ - φᴵ)) on the product of upper half-planes Hⁿ, dropped into the abstract machinery. The metric comes out in closed form, g_{IJ̄} = -δ_{IJ}/(φᴵ - φ̄ᴵ)² (the Poincaré metric), with hermiticity inherited from the abstract proof.

One design choice worth flagging: no doubling. The anti-chiral scalars are the derived conjugates of the chiral fields, never an independent input, so the field space carries the honest number of degrees of freedom, and the physical identities (metric hermiticity, reality of K) hold everywhere rather than only on a reality locus.

Since I'm coming at SUSY from the formalization side, I'd genuinely value review and feedback on #1113 especially. More pieces follow.

My major concern here is the reusability of these chiral label definitions. Since chirality and anti-chirality are common concepts across high-energy physics (like in the Standard Model or general Weyl/Dirac spinor indexing) rather than unique to SUSY, how tightly coupled are these index types to the SUSY machinery? It might be worth ensuring they are defined abstractly enough to be reused elsewhere in Physlib later on.

Good point. A shared "chiral label" definition may well emerge in Physlib eventually, since chirality is not unique to SUSY. For now there is nothing to couple: stripped of names, the file is just Model C A where equiv : C ≃ A (two finite types and a bijection) and ChiralScalarConfiguration C = C → ℂ (a complex field on a finite index), importing only Fintype, Complex, and Equiv from Mathlib. The definitions are already maximally abstract; only the names and the SUSY.N1 namespace are SUSY-specific.

On scope: ChiralScalarConfiguration C = C → ℂ is a single assignment of values to the scalars, not the spacetime-dependent field φ(x). This is deliberate. The Kähler structure here (K, the metric g_{IJ̄} = ∂_I ∂_J̄ K, hermiticity) is geometry on the space of scalar values: ∂_I differentiates with respect to the field values, never x. The dynamical field φ : spacetime → (C → ℂ) and the dynamics using this metric sit strictly on top later, consuming g_{IJ̄} without changing how it is defined.

Once there is a concrete second use, I would be glad to hoist and rename so it can be shaped by that need. Doing it now felt slightly premature for such a small structure, but I am very open to it if you think it is worth doing.
That makes sense. If the structure is already decoupled, leaving it as is until a second use case arises is honestly the best we can do for now. Thanks for the detailed breakdown!

Next review-sized piece is up: the Wirtinger calculus foundation (#1163).

This is the layer underneath everything in the first message. The previous PR was the chiral indexing; this is the differentiation it rests on, split out so it can be reviewed on its own and reused independently of SUSY.

What's in it:

Two files. Basic.lean has the algebraic core, the real-linear decomposition of a map ℂ → ℂ into its holomorphic and anti-holomorphic parts, plus the fact that differentiation commutes with conjugation. Multivariable.lean builds the directional Wirtinger operators ∂_v f and ∂̄_v f on f : V → ℂ over an arbitrary complex vector space, with real-linearity, Leibniz, the two-term chain rule for an outer g : ℂ → ℂ, domain conjugation, and the holomorphic collapse.

The capstone is Schwarz's theorem in Wirtinger form, ∂_v ∂̄_w f = ∂̄_w ∂_v f on a C² field. It's no new analysis, it reduces to the symmetry of the second real Fréchet derivative already in Mathlib (ContDiffAt.isSymmSndFDerivAt). Downstream this is exactly what the Kähler metric's hermiticity, g_{IJ̄} = conj(g_{JĪ}), reduces to.

I'm learning the surrounding math and physics as I go, so corrections and suggestions are very welcome.
